name: Bee venom / snake peptide (Syn-Ake) creams
lead: Bee venom and Syn-Ake creams are cosmetics that borrow from venoms: bee venom products use honeybee venom or its components, while Syn-Ake is a synthetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for wrinkles, named for its design as a mimic of a snake-venom peptide.

Published work on Syn-Ake consists of laboratory and computational studies. A 2024 study used in silico docking and in vitro tests to examine interactions with matrix metalloproteinases and sirtuin 1 and measured antioxidant activity.[1] A 2026 paper described a nanoemulsion formulation of the peptide and evaluated it in silico and in vitro.[2] No human trials were found.

paras: Syn-Ake is a synthetic peptide that appears in anti-ageing formulations; a 2009 patent application lists a Syn-Ake dipeptide among options for a skin cellular synthesis booster in an anti-ageing composition.[3] A 2026 study states that it was developed into a nanoemulsion to reduce wrinkles by affecting neurotransmitters.[2]

Bee venom is a mixture whose largest peptide component is melittin, about 52 percent of venom peptides, alongside phospholipase A2 (about 12 percent), which is identified as a main allergen.[4] Practitioners of apitherapy claim benefits for arthritis, multiple sclerosis and skin conditions, but Wikipedia's article does not cover cosmetic use and reports no clean randomised placebo-controlled trial for arthritis.[4] It also reports that the American Cancer Society says there is no scientific evidence that bee venom therapy treats cancer.[4]

No studies found in humans for Syn-Ake or bee venom creams for wrinkles. Related laboratory research on Syn-Ake exists: in silico and in vitro tests of anti-ageing targets and antioxidant activity,[1] and nanoemulsion formulation work.[2]

card.summary: Venom-mimic creams sold as topical Botox alternatives; only lab data exist.
card.aka: Syn-Ake, bee venom cream, snake venom peptide
card.note: Bee venom contains known allergens; no human wrinkle trials found.

quick.overview:
These creams use bee venom or the synthetic Syn-Ake peptide to promote smoother-looking skin.

Published work is limited to computer and cell-based studies; no human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Syn-Ake is said to act on neurotransmitter signalling to relax expression lines; lab studies also tested effects on matrix metalloproteinases and antioxidant activity.
quick.risks: Bee venom contains allergens such as phospholipase A2. Safety data for Syn-Ake creams in humans were not found in the sources reviewed.
